source_text: κεφαλαίῳ τῷδε, ὅπλα παντοδαπὰ κινοῦντες τοὺς ἀκολάστους λόγους καὶ φάσκοντες συναρπακτικῶς γέγραπται, φησίν· «αἰνεῖτε τὸν κύριον, ὅτι ἀγαθὸν ψαλμός· τῷ θεῷ ἡδυνθείη αἴνεσις,» καί· «ἀγαθὸν τὸ ἐξομολογεῖσθαι τῷ κυρίῳ καὶ ψαλλεῖν τῷ ὀνόματί σου, ὕψιστε.» οὐδαμοῦ δὲ δῆθεν εὑρίσκομεν· αἰνεῖτε τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα. ἀπαντητέον δὲ αὐτοῖς οὕτως· εἰ περὶ τοῦ πατρὸς δέχεσθε, ἃς προεκομίσατε φωνάς, ἐκβάλλετε τὸν υἱόν· εἰ δὲ περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ, τὸ ἐναντίον, ὁπότε καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα κύριός ἐστίν τε καὶ γέγραπται, καὶ ἄδηλον περὶ ποίας ὑποστάσεως γέγραπται νῦν τὸ «κύριος». σκοπεῖτε οὖν, εἰ μὴ τοὐναντίον ἑαυτοῖς ἐχρήσασθε. τὸ δὲ ἅγιον πνεῦμα ὅτι οὐχ ὑμνεῖ, ἐπειδὴ μὴ κτίσμα ἐστίν, συνυμνεῖται δὲ τῷ θεοῦ πνεῦμα ὑπάρχειν ῥᾷον καταμαθεῖν ἀπό τε τοῦ συντάττεσθαι αὐτῷ καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ τοὺς τρεῖς παίδας καὶ τὸν ἱεροψάλτην πᾶσαν τὴν κτίσιν κατ' ὄνομα ὑμνεῖν παρακελεύεσθαι, οὐ μὴν τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ πνεῦμα, ὡς ἔχουσιν συνηθείας οἱ ἅγιοι ἐξονομάσαι. εἰ γάρ, ὡς φασὶν αἱρετικοί, μέσης θεοῦ καὶ ἀγγέλων φύσεώς ἐστιν καὶ τιμιώτερον καὶ ἀνωτέρω πάντων, ἔδει, ἐπειδὴ μάλιστα ἕν ἐστιν, ἢ καθ' ἑαυτὸ παρακελεύσασθαι αὐτὸ ἀνυμνεῖν, ἢ κἂν πρῶτον αὐτὸ ὀνομάσαι καὶ αὐτῷ τὰ ἄλλα γενικῶς συναναλαβεῖν· οὐ μήν, ὡς αὐθαδῶς εἰκάζουσιν, τὸ ἀνάπαλιν. 6.19ν ὅτι μετὰ τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ συνονομάζεται. καὶ περὶ αἱρετικῆς ἀντιθέσεως. ἡ κτίσις οὐ συναριθμεῖται τῷ θεῷ. τί γὰρ καὶ κοινὸν τῇ οὔσῃ ἐν μειώσει πρὸς τὸν πάντων ὑπέρτατον καὶ ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν ὄντα ὑπερβολήν, ἢ τῇ γενομένῃ πρὸς τὸν ποιήσαντα; τὸ δὲ πάντιμον πνεῦμα ὡς θεὸς ἢ μετὰ πατρὸς καὶ υἱοῦ συνονομάζεται, ὡς ὅταν ὁ δεσπότης τὸν περὶ τὸ βάπτισμα δίδωσιν ὅρον, καὶ ὡς ὅταν ὁ ἀπόστολος Κορινθίοις τὸ δεύτερον γράφῃ· «ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, καὶ ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἡ κοινωνία τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν·» ἢ μετὰ μιᾶς αὐτῶν ὑποστάσεως· ἢ καὶ καταμονάς, καθὰ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ εἴρηται βιβλίῳ, μνημονεύεται. ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς προαιρέσεως τοῦ ἐξοβλήτου καὶ ἀπερριμμένου Οὐαλεντίνου τοῦ μανιχαΐσαντος καὶ πρὸς τοῖς ἄλλοις ἀτόποις μυθοπλάσμασιν μανιωδῶς εἰπόντος ἡλικιώτην τὸ θεϊκὸν πνεῦμα τοῖς ἀγγέλοις ὁρμώμενοι οἱ Μακεδονιανοὶ φασίν· Παῦλος Τιμοθέῳ ἔγραψεν· «διαμαρτύρομαι ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ τῶν ἐκ λεκτῶν ἀγγέλων·» τὸ δὲ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, ὡς συντάξας δῆθεν τοῖς ἀγγέλοις, ἀπεσιώπησεν. ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ περισσεύματος τῆς καρδίας αὐτῶν τῆς ἰδίας ἡ ἔννοιά ἐστιν αὕτη. κἂν γάρ ποτε ἰδικῶς μὴ γένηται μνήμη τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος, συναναλαμβάνεται τῷ θεῷ 65 πατρί, ἅτε πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ κατὰ φύσιν ὄν, διά τοι τοῦτό ἐστιν, ὅτε ἢ αὐτὸς ὁ θεὸς πατὴρ τῷ ῥήματι οὐκ ἐμνημονεύθη, ἀλλὰ τῇ πιστῇ διανοίᾳ, ὁ δὲ υἱὸς καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα ἐμνημονεύθη, ἢ τὸ ἔμπαλιν. ὅπου γε μὴ ὀφείλων μνημονεύεσθαι Οὐαλεντῖνος τὸ μὲν ἁγιαστικὸν πνεῦμα «παράκλητον» ὠνόμασεν, ὡς καὶ ὁ δεσπότης Χριστὸς «παράκλητος» ἐκ τοῦ παρακαλεῖσθαι ἐκλήθη· τοὺς δὲ ἁγιαζομένους λειτουργοὺς προσηγόρευσεν «ἀγγέλους». πρὸς τούτοις· οὐδαμοῦ γραφῆς εἰς δημιουργίαν ἢ μυσταγωγίαν ἢ δοξολογίαν ἀγγέλους συμμνημονευομένους εὑρίσκομεν τῷ θεῷ. τοῦ δὲ ἁγίου πνεύματος κοινωνίαν πρὸς τὴν θεότητα ὁ Παῦλος Κορινθίοις ἐν τῇ δευτέρᾳ γέγραφεν ἐπιστολῇ· «ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πατρὸς καὶ ἡ κοινωνία τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος,» καὶ ἐν ἄλλοις· «εἴ τις κοινωνία πνεύματος.» ὁ γοῦν ἱεροψάλτης τὴν πρὸς τὰ λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα ἐξαλλαγὴν τοῦ ἀγενήτου λόγου καὶ τοῦ θεϊκοῦ πνεύματος καὶ τὸ μὴ εἶναι τῆς ἐκείνων συστοιχίας, ἀλλ' ὑπὸ τῶν αὐτοτελῶν ὑποστάσεων τούτων καὶ δι' αὐτῶν καὶ δι' αὐτὰς ὡς καὶ διὰ τὸν θεὸν πατέρα καὶ ἐν αὐταῖς ἐκτίσθαι τοὺς ἀγγέλους καὶ τὰ πάντα τελειοῦσθαι καὶ διακρατεῖσθαι βοᾷ ῥήμασι τοιοῖσδε· «τῷ λόγῳ κυρίου οἱ οὐρανοὶ ἐστερεώθησαν, καὶ τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ στόματος αὐτοῦ πᾶσαι αἱ δυνάμεις αὐτῶν.» νοητέον γὰρ «λόγον» τὸν δι' οὗ τὰ πάντα, «πνεῦμα στόματος κυρίου» τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, «δυνάμεις οὐρανῶν» αὐτάς τε τὰς συστάσεις αὐτῶν, καὶ μέντοι ἀγγέλους καὶ ἀρχὰς καὶ ἐξουσίας καὶ δυνάμεις. καὶ πάλιν· «ὁ ποιῶν τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ πνεύματα, καὶ τοὺς λειτουργοὺς αὐτοῦ πῦρ φλέγον.» διαπληκτίζεται δὲ πρὸς αὐτοὺς καὶ ὁ ἀπόστολος, κράζων· «ἓν πνεῦμα ἐποτίσθημεν.» ὡς γὰρ τὸ ἀπαύγασμα χωρισθῆναι ἀμήχανον τοῦ φωτός, καὶ τὴν σοφίαν τοῦ σοφοῦ, τουτέστιν τὸν υἱὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ πατρός· οὕτως καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα ἀπ' ἐκείνου, οὗ ἐστιν πνεῦμα, ὡς ἡμῖν ὃ
pass_a_gloss: [Continuing from the previous section: ... they set upon even] this chapter, moving as weapons of every kind their unbridled arguments and asserting in a snatching way: it is written, he says: 'praise the Lord, for a psalm is good; to God may praise be sweet,' and: 'it is good to confess to the Lord and to sing to your name, Most High.' But nowhere, forsooth, do we find: praise the Holy Spirit. One must answer them thus: if you receive as about the Father the utterances you brought forward, you cast out the Son; but if about the Son, the opposite, since the Holy Spirit too both is Lord and is written so, and it is unclear about which hypostasis 'Lord' is now written. Consider then whether you have not used [them] against yourselves. And that the Holy Spirit does not hymn, since it is not a creature, but is hymned together by being Spirit of God, is easier to learn both from its being ranked with him and from the three youths and the sacred psalmist exhorting all the creation by name to hymn, but not the Spirit of God, as the saints are accustomed to name [things] out. For if, as heretics say, it is of a nature between God and angels and more honoured and higher than all, it was needful, since it most of all is one, either to exhort it by itself to hymn, or at least to name it first and to take up the others together with it generically; but not, as they presumptuously conjecture, the reverse. 6.19ν [Chapter title:] That it is named together with the Father and the Son. And about a heretical objection. The creation is not counted together with God. For what in common has the one existing in diminution with the one highest of all and being beyond all excess, or the one that came to be with the one who made it? But the all-honoured Spirit as God either is named together with Father and Son, as when the Master gives the rule about baptism, and as when the apostle writes to Corinthians the second time: 'the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit with all of you'; or with one hypostasis of them; or even alone, as was said in the first book, it is mentioned. And starting from the choice of the expelled and cast-off Valentinus, who became a Manichee and, in addition to the other absurd myth-makings, madly said the divine Spirit was of equal age to the angels, the Macedonians say: Paul wrote to Timothy: 'I solemnly charge before God and Lord Jesus Christ and the elect angels'; but the Holy Spirit, as having, forsooth, ranked [it] with the angels, he passed over in silence. But from the abundance of their own heart is this notion. For even if at some time a specific mention of the Holy Spirit does not occur, it is taken up together with God [page number 65, debris] the Father, as being his Spirit by nature; indeed for this reason it is that sometimes either God the Father himself was not mentioned in word, but in the faithful understanding, while the Son and the Holy Spirit were mentioned, or the reverse. Since indeed Valentinus, not deserving to be mentioned, named the sanctifying Spirit 'Paraclete', as also the Master Christ was called 'Paraclete' from being called alongside; but the sanctified ministers he called 'angels'. Besides these: nowhere in Scripture do we find angels mentioned together with God for creating or initiation into the mysteries or doxology. But the fellowship of the Holy Spirit with the Godhead Paul wrote to Corinthians in the second letter: 'the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and Father and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit', and in other places: 'if any fellowship of Spirit'. The sacred psalmist, at any rate, the difference of the uncreated Word and the divine Spirit from the ministering spirits, and their not being of the same row as those, but that by these self-complete hypostases and through them and for their sake, as also for the sake of God the Father, and in them, the angels were created and all things are perfected and held fast, he shouts in such words: 'by the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the breath of his mouth all their powers.' For one must understand 'Word' as the one through whom all things, 'breath of mouth of the Lord' as the Holy Spirit, 'powers of heavens' as both their very structures and indeed angels and principalities and authorities and powers. And again: 'the one making his angels spirits and his ministers a flaming fire.' And the apostle also fights it out against them, crying: 'we were given to drink one Spirit.' For as it is impossible for the radiance to be separated from the light, and the wisdom from the wise, that is, the Son from the Father, so also the Holy Spirit from that one whose Spirit it is, as for us that which [continues in the next section] ...
pass_b_english: …chapter, wielding their unbridled arguments like weapons of every kind and claiming, to snatch assent: “It is written,” they say, “‘Praise the Lord, for a psalm is good; let praise be sweet to God’ (Psalm 147:1), and ‘It is good to give thanks to the Lord and to sing to your name, O Most High’ (Psalm 92:1). But nowhere, if you please, do we find, ‘Praise the Holy Spirit.’”

They must be answered like this. If you take the words you have brought forward as spoken of the Father, you throw out the Son; if as spoken of the Son, the reverse. For the Holy Spirit too both is Lord and is written as Lord, and it is not clear here of which hypostasis “Lord” is written. Consider, then, whether you have not used these texts against yourselves.

That the Holy Spirit does not sing hymns, since he is not a creature, but is hymned together with God because he is the Spirit of God, is easier to learn both from his being ranked with God and from the fact that the three youths and the sacred psalmist bid all creation by name to sing hymns, but not the Spirit of God, though the saints are accustomed to name things one by one. For if, as the heretics say, he is of a nature midway between God and the angels, and more honoured than all and higher than all, then, since he is above all a single being, they ought either to have bidden him by himself to sing hymns, or at least to have named him first and included the rest with him as a class; not, as they presumptuously guess, the very reverse.
That he is named together with the Father and the Son. And on an objection of the heretics.

Creation is not counted together with God. For what does a thing that exists in lessening have in common with him who is highest of all and beyond all excess, or a thing that came to be with him who made it? But the all-honoured Spirit, as God, is named together either with the Father and the Son, as when the Master gives the rule of baptism (Matthew 28:19), and as when the Apostle writes to the Corinthians the second time, “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:14); or with one of their hypostases; or he is mentioned even on his own, as was said in the first book.

Starting from the teaching of the outcast and rejected Valentinus, who turned Manichee and, besides his other absurd fables, said in his madness that the divine Spirit was of an age with the angels, the Macedonians say: “Paul wrote to Timothy, ‘I charge you before God and the Lord Jesus Christ and the elect angels’ (1 Timothy 5:21); but he passed over the Holy Spirit in silence, having, so they claim, ranked him with the angels.” But this notion comes out of the abundance of their own heart (Matthew 12:34).

For even if at times no particular mention is made of the Holy Spirit, he is included with God the Father, since he is his Spirit by nature. That is exactly why there are times when either God the Father himself was not mentioned in words, but only in the believing mind, while the Son and the Holy Spirit were mentioned, or the reverse. Valentinus, indeed, who ought not even to be mentioned, called the sanctifying Spirit “Paraclete,” as the Master Christ too was called “Paraclete” from being called to our side; but the ministers who are sanctified he named “angels.”

Besides this, nowhere in Scripture do we find angels mentioned together with God in the work of creation, or in the rites of initiation, or in the giving of glory. But Paul wrote of the Holy Spirit’s fellowship with the Godhead to the Corinthians in his second letter: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God the Father, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit” (2 Corinthians 13:14); and elsewhere: “If there is any fellowship of the Spirit” (Philippians 2:1).

The sacred psalmist, at any rate, proclaims how the uncreated Word and the divine Spirit differ from the ministering spirits, and that they are not of the same rank as these. Rather, by these self-complete hypostases, and through them, and for their sake, as also for the sake of God the Father, and in them, the angels were created and all things are perfected and held together. He cries out in these words: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the breath of his mouth all their powers” (Psalm 33:6). For by “word” we must understand him through whom all things were made; by “breath of the mouth of the Lord,” the Holy Spirit; and by “powers of the heavens,” both their very frames and also angels, principalities, authorities and powers. And again: “Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flaming fire” (Psalm 104:4).

The Apostle too contends with them, crying out: “We were made to drink of one Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:13). For as it is impossible for the radiance to be parted from the light, and wisdom from the wise, that is, the Son from the Father, so too the Holy Spirit cannot be parted from him whose Spirit he is, just as with us that which …

choices.issue: Garbled draft, dropped chapter title, abbreviated references
choices.choice: 2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix2-e-u16): retranslated. The old English dropped the chapter title 6.19 ('That he is named together with the Father and the Son'), turned Valentinus' 'the Spirit is of an age with the angels' into 'the divine Spirit rushes toward the angels', wrote 'as you perhaps appointed to the angels', 'the Apostle is conflicted toward them', 'substitution of the unbegotten Word' and 'the second [thing]', and put a stray 'that he is named with the Father and the Son' at the end of 6.18. References: (2 Cor 13:13) twice -> 2 Corinthians 13:14 (English numbering); (Ps 33:6), (Ps 104:4), (1 Cor 12:13) written in full; the 'LXX 146:1' label dropped. Brackets '[thing]' and '[the hypostases]' removed.

choices.why: The section opens mid-sentence (the previous section ends ἐπιβαίνουσιν ... καὶ τῷ, 'set upon even the'); only the words this section holds are translated, opened with '…'.
The singular 'he says' reports the Macedonian objector; the English keeps the objection with the opponents.

choices.term: ὡς ἔχουσιν συνηθείας οἱ ἅγιοι ἐξονομάσαι
choices.english: though the saints are accustomed to name things one by one
choices.why: The youths and the psalmist list creatures by name; the point is that their habit of full listing still leaves out the Spirit.

choices.english: since he is above all a single being
choices.why: Contrasts the one Spirit with the many angels; the argument of 6.21 (in the next section) develops it.
That is, leaving him out altogether while naming everything below him.

choices.english: of an age with the angels
choices.why: A peer or contemporary: Valentinus put the Spirit on a level with the angels, which the Macedonians take up.

choices.english: from being called to our side
choices.why: Passive infinitive; Didymus derives 'Paraclete' from the passive sense 'one called alongside'.
ἀγένητος (one nu) means without origin, uncreated; 'unbegotten' (ἀγέννητος) would deny the Son's generation, which Didymus asserts.
Didymus' word for the sacraments, chiefly baptism; 'mysticism' was wrong.

choices.english: breath of his mouth / breath of the mouth of the Lord
choices.why: Psalm 33:6 has πνεῦμα, which Didymus reads as the Holy Spirit; 'breath' is the English sense of the verse and the next sentence says it means the Spirit.
The structures of the heavens themselves, as distinct from the angelic powers.
65 is a printed page number in the copy-text, skipped.

choices.english: just as with us that which …
choices.why: The sentence runs into the next section (ἀναπνέομεν, 'we breathe'); only the words this section holds are translated, ending with '…'.
